Short answer: you do not qualify for this card’s annual-fee rebate for the cardmember year we evaluated. The rebate requires meeting a $7,500 monthly posted-purchase threshold in every one of the 12 monthly windows in the cardmember year; a single month below the threshold disqualifies the whole year. In your case at least one monthly window is below $7,500.

What I checked
- Card: Platinum Rewards Card (account cc_224959b99e_plat)
- Account open date: 11/10/2022 (monthly windows run on the 10th → 9th by posting date)
- Rebate rule: $150 rebate if each monthly window meets $7,500 in net posted purchases
- I reviewed your posted Platinum Rewards Card transactions for the relevant 12-month evaluation period.

Key finding (example)
- Window 11/10/2024–12/09/2024: posted purchases sum = $7,235.26 — this is $264.74 below the $7,500 monthly threshold.
- Because that window is under the threshold, the rebate is not earned for that cardmember year per policy (no partial/prorated rebate).

Next steps I can do for you
- Provide a full month-by-month breakdown for the cardmember year so you can see each window’s posted total and exactly which window(s) missed the threshold.
- If you believe a posted transaction was incorrectly excluded (e.g., a purchase posted in a different month, or a disputed/returned charge affected totals), I can review specific transactions with you and advise on next steps.
- If you’d like human help to escalate (for example if you think the rebate was applied but is missing), I can transfer you to a specialist — would you like that?

Good questions — here’s how to decide and what to enter so your application is accurate and best for underwriting.

Employment status: Self‑employed vs Employed
- Choose Self‑employed if you operate as an independent contractor, freelancer, sole proprietor, or run your own business (even if it’s a one‑person operation). That’s the correct choice when you don’t receive a W‑2 from an employer.
- Choose Employed only if you have a regular employer who pays you (W‑2), even if you also do some freelance work on the side.

Why it matters
- Underwriters expect truthful reporting. Marking Self‑employed when that’s your situation avoids mismatches if they verify income or look at tax records.
- If you have a single large client but are paid as a contractor (1099), you should still select Self‑employed.

What to put for employer/business name
- If self‑employed, enter your business name (if you have one). If you don’t have a formal business name, use “Yuki Nakamura” or “Yuki Nakamura, Graphic Design” or simply “Self‑Employed.”
- If you’re employed by a company and have a job title there, list that employer’s legal name.

Income reporting
- For annual income, enter your total gross income that you expect underwriters to consider (you told me $95,000). For self‑employed applicants, that’s typically gross business income before expenses (or the number you report on taxes) — use the figure that best matches what you report on your tax return.
- If the form asks for monthly income, divide accordingly ($95,000 ÷ 12 ≈ $7,916.67 per month).

Other income
- Leave “other income” blank if you don’t have consistent, verifiable additional income (rental, alimony, investment income, etc.). Don’t invent amounts — underwriters may ask for documentation if it’s material.
- If you have small, irregular side income that’s not consistent or not reported, it’s safer to leave it out.
